claims.text: The as-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a fine FCC matrix.
The as-built alloy has a high dislocation density.
The as-built alloy has minimal pre-existing oxide scale and minimal cracking.
Degradation during high-temperature gas exposure is governed by formation and evolution of a brittle intergranular oxide scale.
The governing oxide scale is predominantly TiO2 and Al2O3, with contributions from chromium oxides.
Oxide formation occurs preferentially at grain boundaries and defect sites.
The oxide-scale morphology is susceptible to spallation.
High-density additive-manufacturing defects accelerate surface oxidation at elevated temperature.
In an oxidizing atmosphere, a continuous mixed-phase oxide layer develops substantial thermal and residual stresses.
Oxide-scale stresses cause cracking and spallation and concentrate stress sufficiently to nucleate cracks.
Under reducing gas conditions, incomplete or unstable oxide formation permits internal oxidation and additional microstructural degradation.
Oxidizing and reducing exposure routes both reduce mechanical integrity and can promote catastrophic failure.
Relative to the as-built baseline, oxidizing exposure will produce a thicker, continuous but cracked and spalled oxide scale.
Oxidizing exposure will increase grain-boundary crack density and markedly decrease high-temperature strength.
Reducing exposure will produce incomplete oxide protection, internal oxidation, microcracking, and deteriorated mechanical properties.
The proposed mechanism operates specifically from 700 to 900 °C during approximately 100 to 500 hours of controlled gas exposure.
At lower temperatures or in inert atmospheres, oxidation kinetics and associated stress development may be insufficient to trigger catastrophic failure.
Changing the atmosphere between oxidizing and reducing conditions at fixed temperature provides a controlled test of oxide-scale-mediated degradation.
The atmosphere-dependent behavior can be evaluated by measuring oxide thickness and composition, grain-boundary crack density, residual stress, and high-temperature mechanical properties.

The hypothesis is falsified if atmosphere variation produces no statistically significant and reproducible differences in oxide formation, crack density, or mechanical deterioration relative to baseline.
